name: Liliʻuokalani
info: Liliʻuokalani was the only queen regnant and last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, ruling from 1891 until her overthrow in 1893, and the composer of "Aloha ʻOe" and author of a memoir of her country.

facts.born: 2 September 1838, at the base of Punchbowl Crater in Honolulu, Oʻahu; daughter of Analea Keohokālole and Caesar Kapaʻakea, of the aliʻi class, adopted at birth by Abner Pākī and Laura Kōnia
facts.died: 11 November 1917, at her residence, Washington Place, in Honolulu, aged seventy-nine, after several months of deteriorating health
facts.role: Princess (from 1874) and heir apparent to the Hawaiian throne (1877–1891); regent (1881 and 1890–1891); Queen of the Hawaiian Kingdom (29 January 1891 – 17 January 1893)
facts.known: The only queen regnant and last monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom; her attempt to replace the Bayonet Constitution; her overthrow in 1893 and forced abdication in 1895; opposing the annexation of Hawaiʻi by the United States; composing "Aloha ʻOe"; her memoir Hawaiʻi's Story by Hawaiʻi's Queen; her translation of the Kumulipo

t: Raised among the Hawaiian nobility and schooled by American missionaries, Liliʻuokalani became heir apparent in 1877 and queen in 1891, the only woman to reign over the Hawaiian Kingdom.

Her attempt to proclaim a constitution restoring the powers of the monarchy and the votes of disenfranchised Hawaiians and Asians led a Committee of Safety, backed by the landing of United States forces, to depose her in January 1893.
Imprisoned and made to abdicate in 1895, she spent years protesting annexation and seeking the return of the Crown Lands, and is remembered also as a composer and writer.
dyk: Following Hawaiian custom, she was named after an event at her birth: the regent Elizabeth Kīnaʻu had an eye infection, and gave the child names meaning smarting, tearful, a burning pain and sore eyes. The name Liliʻuokalani, "the smarting of the royal ones", dates from 1877.
ev: Lydia Liliʻu Loloku Walania Kamakaʻeha is born on 2 September in Honolulu, on the island of Oʻahu
She marries the American-born John Owen Dominis on 16 September and moves into Washington Place in Honolulu
After the death of her brother Leleiohoku she is designated heir apparent on 10 April and given the name Liliʻuokalani by King Kalākaua
She takes the oath of office on 29 January, nine days after Kalākaua's death, as the first and only female monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom
She is deposed on 17 January and a provisional government under Sanford B. Dole is recognised by the United States minister John L. Stevens
Arrested after a failed royalist rebellion, she signs a document of abdication on 24 January in return for the release of her jailed supporters
Hawaiʻi is annexed by the United States through the Newlands Resolution; she boycotts the ceremony of 12 August and publishes her memoir
She dies on 11 November at Washington Place and receives a state funeral in the throne room of ʻIolani Palace

sections.early:
Liliʻuokalani was born Lydia Liliʻu Loloku Walania Kamakaʻeha on 2 September 1838, in the grass house of her maternal grandfather ʻAikanaka at the base of Punchbowl Crater in Honolulu, on Oʻahu. Her parents, Analea Keohokālole and Caesar Kapaʻakea, were of the aliʻi class of the Hawaiian nobility, collateral relations of the reigning House of Kamehameha and descendants of two of the five royal counsellors of Kamehameha I. She was the third surviving child of a large family that included David Kalākaua, Miriam Likelike and William Pitt Leleiohoku II. By the custom of hānai, an informal adoption within extended families, she was given at birth to Abner Pākī and his wife Laura Kōnia and raised with their daughter Bernice Pauahi.

In 1842, aged four, she entered the Chiefs' Children's School, later the Royal School, whose pupils Kamehameha III had formally proclaimed eligible for the throne. The American missionaries Amos Starr Cooke and Juliette Montague Cooke taught her and her royal cousins in English. She later looked back on those years unfavourably, remembering being "sent hungry to bed" and the measles epidemic of 1848 that killed a classmate and her younger sister Kaʻiminaʻauao. After the boarding school closed around 1850 she attended a day school and lived with her hānai parents at Haleʻākala. Pākī died in 1855 and Kōnia two years later, and she came under the guardianship of Bernice Pauahi and her American husband, Charles Reed Bishop. At the court of Kamehameha IV she was a close friend and attendant of Queen Emma.
sections.rise:
After a brief engagement to William Charles Lunalilo, which she broke off, she married the American-born John Owen Dominis, a secretary to Kamehameha IV, on 16 September 1862. The marriage was reportedly unhappy; the couple had no children of their own, and she adopted three hānai children. She kept her place at court and in 1866 composed "He Mele Lāhui Hawaiʻi" as a national anthem at the request of Kamehameha V. When Lunalilo, the first elected king, died without an heir in 1874, the legislature chose her brother David Kalākaua over the dowager queen Emma, a result that caused a riot at the courthouse. Kalākaua gave his siblings royal titles and named their brother Leleiohoku heir.

Leleiohoku died in 1877, and on 10 April she was designated heir apparent; Kalākaua then changed her name to Liliʻuokalani. She served as regent during his world tour of 1881, when she met a smallpox epidemic by closing the ports and imposing a quarantine; there were 789 cases and 289 deaths, mainly among Native Hawaiians. She visited the Kalaupapa leper settlement, founded a savings bank for women and an educational society for Hawaiian girls in 1886, and in 1887 attended Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee in London. There she learned that Kalākaua had been forced, under threat of death, to sign the Bayonet Constitution. She was regent again from November 1890, when the king left for California. He died in San Francisco on 20 January 1891; the news reached Honolulu on 29 January, and she took the oath of office that day.
sections.deeds:
Liliʻuokalani began her reign by requiring the resignation of her brother's cabinet, a step the Supreme Court upheld with one dissent. On 9 March 1891 she named her niece Kaʻiulani as successor, and from April to July she toured the main islands. Her husband, made Prince Consort and restored as Governor of Oʻahu, died on 27 August 1891. From May 1892 to January 1893 the legislature sat for an unprecedented 171 days, divided among four parties; under the constitution of 1887 it could dismiss her ministers, and it voted out four of her cabinets.

From early in her reign she received petitions to rewrite the Bayonet Constitution, a demand supported by two-thirds of the registered voters. With the legislators Joseph Nāwahī and William Pūnohu White she drafted a constitution that would have restored power to the monarchy and voting rights to economically disenfranchised Native Hawaiians and Asians. On 13 January 1893 she appointed a cabinet chosen to support its promulgation, but her ministers withheld their backing, and on 16 January she and her supporters abandoned the attempt to proclaim it unilaterally. She was deposed the next day. She yielded her authority temporarily to the United States, not to the provisional government, in the hope that Washington would restore Hawaiian sovereignty. She was also an author and songwriter: she wrote "Aloha ʻOe", translated the creation chant Kumulipo, published in 1897, and set out her view of her country's history in Hawaiʻi's Story by Hawaiʻi's Queen (1898).
sections.opponents:
Her opponents were led by Lorrin A. Thurston, a grandson of American missionaries, and William Owen Smith. Calling her constitutional plan "revolutionary", they formed a 13-member Committee of Safety that drew its support mainly from the American and European business class and aimed to depose the queen and seek annexation to the United States. Her own ministers and closest friends had opposed the plan and tried to dissuade her. When the Marshal of the Kingdom, Charles Burnett Wilson, asked for warrants to arrest the committee, the cabinet refused, fearing escalation. Marines and sailors from the USS Boston landed; they fired no shot, but their presence intimidated the royalist defenders. The historian William Russ states that "the injunction to prevent fighting of any kind made it impossible for the monarchy to protect itself".

American judgements were divided. The Blount Report, commissioned by President Grover Cleveland, concluded that the overthrow was illegal and that the minister John L. Stevens and American troops had acted inappropriately; the Senate's Morgan Report of 26 February 1894 found Stevens and all parties except the queen "not guilty". Cleveland offered to restore her if she granted an amnesty. Her first reply, that Hawaiian law prescribed confiscation of property and death for treason and that only her ministers could set it aside, lost her the goodwill of his administration, and when she changed her position the provisional government refused to reinstate her.
sections.last:
The provisional government became the Republic of Hawaii on 4 July 1894, with Sanford B. Dole as president. In January 1895 Robert W. Wilcox and Samuel Nowlein led a rebellion to restore the monarchy. It failed, and on 16 January Liliʻuokalani was arrested and confined in an upstairs bedroom of ʻIolani Palace after firearms were found at Washington Place. On 24 January she signed a document of abdication in return for the release of her jailed supporters, six of whom had been sentenced to hang; she wrote later that she would have chosen death for herself. A military commission tried her in the throne room on 8 February and sentenced her to five years of hard labour and a fine of $5,000, commuted on 4 September to imprisonment in the palace. On 13 October 1896 the Republic gave her a full pardon.

She then divided her time between Hawaii and Washington, D.C. In 1897 she filed a formal protest against a new annexation treaty, which failed in the Senate after Native Hawaiian delegates presented petitions bearing over 21,000 signatures. Hawaii was annexed all the same by the Newlands Resolution in July 1898, and she and her household stayed away from the ceremony of 12 August. For more than a decade she sought recompense for the Crown Lands seized by the United States; her lawsuit of 1909 failed, and in 1911 the Territory of Hawaii granted her a pension of $1,250 a month. She died there on the morning of 11 November 1917, aged seventy-nine, and after a state funeral on 18 November was entombed in the Royal Mausoleum at Mauna ʻAla.
sections.legacy:
Liliʻuokalani's reign ended the Hawaiian monarchy, and the lands once reserved for it passed to the territorial government, the source of the "Ceded Lands" issue in Hawaii. The historian Sydney Lehua Iaukea noted that the pension granted her in 1911 never addressed the legality of the seizure. By her will the Queen Liliʻuokalani Trust, established on 2 December 1909, received most of her estate for the care of orphaned and destitute children; lawsuits against it, one brought by Prince Jonah Kūhiō Kalanianaʻole in 1915, were resolved in 1923. Newspapers in Hawaii that had supported the overthrow acknowledged at her death the esteem in which she was held around the world.

Her music helped preserve traditional Hawaiian poetics while taking up the Western harmonies the missionaries had brought. "Aloha ʻOe", written as a lover's farewell and transcribed during her confinement, came to be regarded as a lament for the loss of her country and is among the most recognisable Hawaiian songs; a collection, The Queen's Songbook, appeared in 1999. The Hawaiian Music Hall of Fame honours her and her siblings as Na Lani ʻEhā, "The Heavenly Four". An outrigger canoe race, hula competitions and a festival in Hilo bear her name, and in 2001 the regents of the University of Hawaii described her as "an important link to traditional Hawaiian culture and society". On 19 January 2026 the Episcopal Church formally recognised her as a saint at her resting place, honouring her decision to avoid bloodshed during the overthrow.

summary: Liliʻuokalani, born into the Hawaiian nobility in 1838, reigned as the last monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom from 1891 to 1893. Her attempt to proclaim a new constitution brought her overthrow by annexationists backed by United States forces; she was later imprisoned, abdicated under duress and opposed annexation. She is remembered too as the composer of "Aloha ʻOe".

Allan Seiden, Liliʻuokalani: A Royal Album (Mutual Publishing, 2017)

notes: The article writes dates month-first. Event date column: years only; event sentences keep the article's month-first form; facts and sections are day-first as on the rest of the site. Editor to make uniform if wanted.

Committee of Safety: the lead says seven foreign residents (five Americans, one Scotsman, one German) and six Hawaiian Kingdom subjects of American descent; the body says six Hawaiian citizens, five US citizens, one British citizen and one German citizen, and '13-member council'. I wrote only '13-member'.

The memoir: the lead says she wrote it 'during her imprisonment following the overthrow'; the body says it was written with Julius A. Palmer's help after her 1896 release and published in 1898. I gave only the publication year.
Dominis: the article calls him 'a staff member for Prince Lot Kapuāiwa and secretary to King Kamehameha IV'; I wrote 'a secretary to Kamehameha IV'.

'Her husband ... died on 27 August 1891': the article says 'August 27, seven months into her reign'; the year follows from that. Likewise '9 March 1891' and 'April to July' are given without a year, in the paragraph on the start of her reign.
'She yielded her authority temporarily to the United States': the article says 'She temporarily relinquished her throne to the United States, rather than the Dole-led government'.

'the lands once reserved for it passed to the territorial government': article - Crown Lands were seized by the United States government at annexation, and the territorial government took control under the Organic Act of 1900.
Kumulipo: the article gives 'the 1897 publication of the Kumulipo translation'.
Regent dates in the titles list: January 20, 1881 - October 29, 1881, and November 25, 1890 - January 29, 1891.
Honolulu magazine's 2007 rating of 'Aloha ʻOe' as 'the greatest song in the history of Hawaiian music' was left out (the guide's word list).

The article spells the islands 'Hawaii' and 'Hawaiʻi' by turns; I kept 'Republic of Hawaii', 'Territory of Hawaii', 'University of Hawaii' as the article has them and used Hawaiʻi in the info, facts and takeaways as its lead does.
Her 1906 Latter-day Saint baptism and 1896 Anglican confirmation were left out for length.

Left out for length (all in the article): the Reform Party approach of December 20 and 23 (year not stated in the article; Kuykendall: a conditional answer, her own account: a firm refusal); her raising of the American flag in April 1917 for the sailors of the SS Aztec, whose meaning historians dispute; her attendance at the Buddha's Birthday celebration of 1901; the lottery and opium bills of the 1892 legislature.
The article names no successor to her claim after 1893 beyond Kaʻiulani (named heir on March 9, 1891); the succession is therefore not treated in the last section.
